newsitem.title: UK: Greenpeace credit card, your biodegradeable friend.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace credit card, your biodegradeable friend.

text.p: Buried treasure took on a new meaning on Wednesday when environmental group Greenpeace and Britain's Co-operative Bank launched the world's first biodegradeable credit card.
"Every customer of every bank worldwide will be carrying a biodegradeable card within 10 years," the bank's managing director Terry Thomas told Reuters after the launch of the Visa card.

Greenpeace decided to issue the card -- which is made of a plastic produced from natural resources such as wheat and sugar and in the right conditions biodegrades naturally into water and carbon dioxide -- as part of its campaign against the use of PVC.

Until now cards have been made of the oil-derived plastic and the new card is the first to be made of Biopol. This has been created by U.S. chemicals giant Monsanto and has passed tests by the bank and conforms with Visa's criteria. When buried in a compost heap the card, which is 99.9 percent PVC free, decomposes quickly.
A sample had largely disintegrated into a pile of earth after a mere eight weeks. But unless there are micro-organisms there to do the work, the card will not decompose in your pocket.
Lord Melchett, director of Greenpeace, told Reuters he had been campaigning against the manufacture, use and disposal of PVC (polyvinyl chloride) for years.

Greenpeace, known around the globe for its high-profile direct action environmental campaigning, argues that PVC production and disposal involves the release of large quantities of carcinogenic and hormone-disrupting chemicals into the environment.
"This is going to be a tremendous tool to inform people about the dangers and the solution to PVC production," Melchett said.

Brandishing the new card, which features a picture of Greenpeace's flagship the Rainbow Warrior and the motto "this card proves there is an alternative to PVC", Melchett said it represented a serious threat to PVC producers.
"This is more of a threat than blocking a chemical outfall pipe," he said, adding that the Co-operative Bank had been inundated with calls about following newspaper advertisements for the card.

Despite an apparently unlikely alliance with Monsanto, which Greenpeace has campaigned against because of its development of genetically modified soymeal, Melchett said he had no qualms about using the Biopol technology or teaming up with the group.

"We will continue to campaign against the use of genetically engineered foodstuffs," he said, adding Greenpeace did not campaign against companies but against what they did if it damaged the environment.
Although relatively small, the Co-op Bank has gained widespread publicity for its environmental and ethical approach to banking, differentiating itself from Britain's other high street banks.

Thomas said the bank is committed to replacing all of its existing two million credit and debit cards with Biopol cards by the year 2000 despite the fact that at the moment it costs more than the PVC.
At present expired cards are either placed in a landfill site or burned, thus releasing PVC by-products into the environment. Greenpeace says that around 20 million tonnes of PVC are produced a year.

The Co-op Bank says there are 500 million credit cards in circulation around the world which if laid end to end would circle the globe. This does not include other uses of PVC such as debit cards, store cards, reward cards and telephone cards.

As with the Co-op Bank's other affinity cards -- which are offered with a no annual fee for life pledge -- Greenpeace will get a five pound donation from the bank for every Visa card issued as well as 25 pence for every 100 pounds ($164) spent.
Greenpeace estimates it could raise around 200,000 pounds a year if just 10 percent of its 200,000 supporters take out a card and spend on it.
And Credit cards are just one of the many possible applications for Biopol, according to Monsanto's Biopol marketing manager Malcolm Forsyth.
But Forsyth told Reuters he did not expect the product to become cheaper than its petro-chemical based predecessor in the near future.
Despite this, Forsyth says others will follow the lead of NBS Card Services which has produced the Greenpeace card, and opt for "green" polymer cards.

Cosmetic bottles, drink cups and water filters have already been commercially produced in Europe and Japan and Forsyth said more products, particularly food packaging, are in the pipeline. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
